title: Toyota Yaris Rear Drum Brakes: Wheel Cylinder Leak, Line Replacement, and Bleeding
summary: This video provides an in-depth, hands-on repair of a Toyota Yaris rear drum brake system affected by a leaking wheel cylinder that contaminated the rear shoes. The host documents diagnosing no braking, replacing the leaking wheel cylinder, replacing rusty brake lines, cleaning contaminated components, installing new shoes and hardware, and bleeding the system via gravity and pedal methods. A test drive checks whether the master cylinder survived the service, with notes on a common Toyota quirk where the brake warning float can stick when fluid is low. The walkthrough emphasizes practical decisions when budget constraints exist (such as preserving a compromised backing plate) and cautions against fabricating hard lines in favor of OEM pre-bent parts. Throughout, the guide highlights key drum-brake concepts—shoe and star wheel adjustment, hydraulic threading, and iterative checks—to ensure safe, functional brakes after the repair.

title: LS400 Parts Cannon: Misdiagnosis and Root-Cause Fix
summary: The Car Care Nut video recounts a pristine Lexus LS400 that suffered severe vibration and shake when accelerating, which was repeatedly worsened by a string of aftermarket parts and misdiagnoses. The host traces the problem back to original engine and transmission mounts, which were replaced with aftermarket units, and demonstrates how this cascade led to drive shaft and rear-end modifications that failed to solve the root cause. Through hands-on diagnosis, swapping in a known-good driveshaft, and comparing parts, the video illustrates a methodical backtracking approach to root-cause analysis, the challenges of sourcing original LS400 parts, and a call for using factory parts (where appropriate) to preserve the car’s integrity. It also highlights broader issues in independent shops’ part sourcing and emphasizes the importance of preserving LS400-era components via heritage-part programs.

title: Toyota Sienna 2GR-FE Harness Replacement After Rodent Damage (ECU/ECU and Engine Wiring)
summary: The Car Care Nut walks through a high-stakes harness replacement on a 2011 Toyota Sienna affected by severe rodent damage that fried injector drivers and the engine computer. It details the arduous process of accessing and removing a stubborn belt-driven compressor to reach a crank sensor behind it, managing a tangle of brackets and connectors, and then installing a brand-new engine harness with careful attention to routing and orientation. The overall message emphasizes the importance of identifying proper, complete harness repairs rather than piecemeal fixes that leave the vehicle prone to future failure.

title: Diagnosis and Troubleshooting of Toyota/Lexus Parking Sensor ICS Wiring and Calibration
summary: The Car Care Nut’s video explains Toyota and Lexus Intelligent Clearance Sensors (ICS) parking systems, focusing on how these sensors are wired in a daisy-chained network and how to diagnose faults without blindly replacing components. The host details front/rear sensor separation, six-pin sensor design, and the three-wire-per-end architecture (ground plus two communications). He demonstrates practical diagnostic steps: testing continuity from the harness to individual sensors, recognizing that a single faulty sensor can disrupt the entire network, and the importance of using a known-good sensor to isolate failures. The video also covers calibration via bi-directional scan tools, interpretation of common codes such as C1AED, harness fragility near the exhaust, and pragmatic advice to consider replacing the harness when diagnosing. The overall emphasis is understanding how the ICS network operates before diagnosing to avoid misleading conclusions and extended diagnostics.

title: HVAC Actuator Rescue on a 2013 Lexus RX350: Dual-Servo, One-Unit Design, and the Perils of DIY Repair
summary: The video documents a repair attempt on a 2013 Lexus RX350’s climate-control system that centers on a single, integrated actuator unit containing two servo motors (one for mode/air distribution and one for temperature). Across the teardown, the discussion shifts to the broader design philosophy between automotive engineers and mechanics, the difficulty of aligning multiple tiny arms, the challenge of accessing the HVAC box behind the dash, and the risks of damaging the HVAC box or wiring harnesses. A donor car is used to help set the actuator in the correct position, followed by testing with a known-good unit. The host emphasizes meticulous organization (bolts and harnesses), adherence to the repair manual, and a caution against DIYing complex interior repairs or cutting corners, ending with a recap of lessons learned and practical guidance for viewers.

title: Toyota 2019 4Runner AC Diagnosis: Evaporator Freeze, Expansion Valve, and Sleepless Nights
summary: The Car Care Nut documents an intermittent air conditioning failure on a 2019 Toyota 4Runner (fifth generation) that only surfaces after extended driving. The shop pursues an ambitious dash-disassembly route to access the evaporator and expansion valve, uncovers rodent damage to the dash harness, and unfolds a multi-day diagnostic saga. Initial testing shows normal pressures, but the evaporator frost progresses with longer drives. The team suspects the expansion valve, replaces the evaporator assembly, and tests with gauges; eventual trouble resurfaces due to a misadjusted compressor clutch air gap and an aging “ID box” security harness, prompting a second round of repair. The video chronicles a roller-coaster process—from dash removal and harness diagnostics to compressor clutch shim adjustments and a recalibrated replacement valve—culminating in a resolved system and reflections on the challenges of intermittent AC faults, customer communication, and shop ethics. The narrative is anchored by live-shop footage and day-by-day progression rather than a single, clean-in-one-go repair.

title: Toyota Celica 1995 AC Pulley Repair: Pulley-Only Replacement, Shim Gaps, and Reassembly
summary: In this episode, The Car Care Nut examines a near-mint 1995 Toyota Celica Convertible with about 41,000 miles that is making an AC-related noise. Rather than replacing the entire compressor, he isolates the sound to the compressor pulley and demonstrates a pulley-only repair strategy. The process includes removing the compressor, bench-assembling and inspecting the clutch, explaining how the magnetic clutch works, measuring the clutch gap with a dial indicator, and selecting and installing shims to achieve the spec (~20 thousandths clearance). After validating the gap, he reinstalls the compressor, belts, and lines, charges the AC system, performs an oil and filter change on the 5S engine, and concludes with a tour of the car’s original condition and its maintenance history. The video blends diagnostic reasoning, careful parts selection in the face of scarce vintage parts, and practical, tool-based steps to service aging automotive hardware while preserving originality.

title: 2GR-FE ES350 Diagnostic Odyssey: Counterfeit Parts, Calculated Load, and a Blocked Catalytic Converter
summary: This video chronicles a diagnostic odyssey on a 2013 Lexus ES350 (2GR-FE) with about 150,000 miles, where the team confronts a stubborn power-loss symptom that appears after a transmission replacement. Despite swapping counterfeit ignition coils, a counterfeit throttle body, and even the engine computer, and performing tests from fuel pressure to vacuum, the car gives no codes and misfires intermittently. After exhausting numerous hypotheses and even scheduling “timeouts,” the investigators discover a pivotal clue in the calculated load data, then compare with a similar Toyota Camry to identify a blocked catalytic converter as the root cause. A bottom-inspection reveals the honeycomb is partially collapsed, confirming the blockage. The video also discusses the impracticality of complete exhaust replacement and the owner’s decision not to fix the car, but emphasizes a key diagnostic takeaway: relying on calculated load and bottom-side catalytic converter inspection can be essential when vacuum and backpressure tests are inconclusive on modern Toyota engines.
